Name: Bob Hannent
Question: Why hasn't NASA brought an HD video camera or an iPhone to the moon to record 4k or HD videos? Isn't anybody curious to how it would look?
Answer: Firstly, it’s important to recognise that there hasn’t been much in the way of traffic between the Earth and the moon, especially for NASA, since the last moon landing in 1972. But one organisation did send an HD camera to the Moon in the first decade of the 2000s. JAXA (the Japanese space agency) sent one into low moon orbit in 2007. I actually saw this in its full quality HD, on a professional projector, thanks to NHK and I can tell you YouTube doesn’t do it justice. Search JAXA KAGUYA. There’s also been the NASA LRO (Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter) which arrived at the moon in 2009 but spent +11 years studying the moon.

Name: Bob Hannent
Question: How come China has not figured out how to produce an OLED TV?
Answer: Fabrication of TV panels is really, really, really hard and requires massive investment. I seem to recall that the lg OLED factory cost then over $3bn to build and that's the risk they took before they knew they could get good yields in mass production. Making an OLED panel is like making a 55in chip and expecting zero defects. Getting that kind of low failure rate has been critical to LG and it's why Sony didn't scale their OLED technology. Sony still manufactures limited runs of small OLED displays for professional/broadcast products but all their OLED TVs are LG panels. You can count on one hand the number of companies fabricating UHD panels of any kind, let alone OLED. Even if another company figured out how to make OLED panels, they have to compete with an existing manufacturer who likely has better yield, better economy of scale, already has the customers and over a decade of experience. That's not a fight I'd go looking for in a market where profit margins are razor thin. Remember that LG Display (the company that makes the panels) isn't profitable.

Name: Bob Hannent
Question: A lot of paid streaming services are tanking. Is this the same with free streaming services such as Tubi or Pluto TV?
Answer: There's a lot of analytics which people are pointing to which is showing that there's a market saturation point for consumers and by the same token they're saying that if you're not winning you're losing. But the reality is that it should be possible to coexist and run businesses without being told that you're going to die just because you're not growing exponentially. However, I'll also say that it's really, really hard to do streaming well AND make a profit. Also, I don't think Disney was right to gatekeep it's content instead of keeping on syndicating it. The idea of keeping a bigger slice of the pie by owning and operating your own platform is fine, but the reality is that it restricted their audience. There's a threshold of the number of services that people are willing to subscribe to and how much they will spend each month, so a portion of the audience who will watch a piece of content will just forget about it unless it's on the platforms they otherwise have. Not everyone who likes (not loves, likes) Marvel films will pay extra to watch them. So there's a lost generation by gatekeeping. Running the distribution infrastructure, the content management systems, the payment processing, the customer service system, the many app development teams AND the anti-piracy systems is expensive.

Question: Why do movies or TV shows on television play at one volume, but when commercials come on, they play at higher or ridiculous volumes?
Answer: It's so that the adverts grab your attention, weirdly they aren't necessarily a higher volume but they are “Louder” with some clever audio techniques. In the USA this is actually against the FCC guidelines after the CALM Act of 2011. There is a process for complaining: "Federal Communications Commission" Loud Commercials.

Name: Bob Hannent
Question: Why do I get no signal window when I get perfect picture on Samsung TV (dvi to hdmi)?
Answer: Sometimes a display shows a picture AND an error when there’s something wrong with the input video that the TV can’t quite understand. It’s more of a bug than a failure. In this case, it’s probably some kind of communication issue between the TV and the source device. With DVI and HDMI there’s a process called EDID where the sink (the TV) talks to the source and asks it what formats it supports. Then the response is used to decide how to display the video signal that gets sent. If the TV doesn’t like the EDID or the source offers formats that it doesn’t think it can display, it’ll put an error on the screen. But if so, why is it displaying a picture? Because the brains of the TV think it cannot, but the actual display processor, which is a separate component, somehow managed it. Or because the picture isn’t as perfect as you might think. For example there might be timing and alignment issues which you haven’t noticed and the TV is making a best effort at displaying it but it knows the video is being clipped (for example) or some other artefact is happening. It could just be that the source is sending no EDID, or the EDID is corrupt and the TV is showing an error because of this, but the display processor is happily showing whatever it found.
